links.reason: Both Paranar courtesan poems close on the same demand (என் நலம்தந்து சென்மே, 396.19 / 376.18) and both use the Kaviri hiding Aththi (காவிரி கொண்டொளித் தாங்கு 396.14 / 376.11). In 396 the tenor is spelled out (நின் மனையோள் வவ்வலும் அஞ்சுவல், 15), while 376 leaves it implicit after மன்னோ, so the pair shows the legend fixed as a figure for the wife's hold. 'Lawful' is the marker's gloss, but the core claim holds.

241 only shows the giver of chariots (திண்தேர் இரவலர்க்கு ஈத்த) welcomed in Indra's hall; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world (மேலுலகம் இல்லெனினும்). The couplet does not deny the reward 241 pictures, so the claims are not incompatible; it detaches value from reward, a qualification. That the couplet 'deliberately' answers such praise poems is not shown by either text.

319's wife with the jar emptied (வறிது, 4) offers roasted hare (முயல்சுட்ட வாயினும் தருகுவேம், 8) and promises the unfading lotus later, which is the converse of 89's உடைமையுள் இன்மை. The poem illustrates rather than limits the couplet, since 89 already makes hospitality a matter of use, not stores; the teaches sentence largely restates that.

234 contrasts the small rice ball on grass (இன்சிறு பிண்டம், 4) with Evvi's habit of eating with many (பலரோடு உண்டல் மரீஇ யோனே, 6), and 229 makes solitary eating (தமியர் உணல்) worse than begging. The poem never says he eats alone, only that the offering is small and from one hand, and it does not limit the Kural's claim about hoarders; the pairing is a suggestive shared image, not a qualification.

The only bond is the word புற்கை: in 84 the lord eats gruel yet has broad shoulders (புற்கை யுண்டும் பெருந்தோ ளன்னே), in 1065 gruel earned by one's own effort (தாள்தந்தது) is sweetest. The couplet's point is self-reliance in poverty; nothing in it draws on a heroic image, so the claim that it 'draws on' 84 is unsupported. Line 1's என்ஜ is a corrupt spelling.
links.text_issue: purananuru:84 line 1 என்ஜ is corrupt (for என்னை)

links.reason: Both name Karikal's battle at Venni (வெண்ணி வாயில் 246.9; வெண்ணிப் பறந்தலை 66.6). 66 tells the victor the dead loser is the better man (நின்னினும் நல்லன் அன்றே), while 246 uses only the victory roar at Azhundur (அழுந்தூர் ஆர்ப்பினும் பெரிதே) as a scale for gossip; the note says exactly what the akam poet does with the battle.

109's four yields are things the hill gives unploughed (உழவர் உழாதன நான்கு பயன்); 303's sparrows of Parambu fly out at dawn for red paddy and return at dusk (காலைப் போகி ... செந்நெல் தரீஇயர் ... மாலைப் படர்தந் தாங்கு), a simile of sure return, not of food without farming. The common element 'food coming in without farming' is constructed; the real shared thread, Pari's giving (303.8-10; 109.18), is not what the note uses.

367 states the premise that possessions do not go with their owners (தம்மொடு செல்லா) and only good deeds are a raft (நல்வினை அல்லது ... புணைபிறிது இல்லை); Naladiyar 120 says only one's deeds go along (தாஞ்செய் வினையல்லால் தம்மொடு செல்வது ... இல்லை) and the adorned body is useless. From the same premise 367 draws drinking (நாரறி தேறல் மாந்தி) and lavish gifts, while 120 disparages the cherished body, so the pair shows the doctrine did not fix one conclusion. 'Jain anthology' generalises past verse 120, a minor overreach.

287 does make the high world the reward and waves away land (தண்ணடை பெறுதல் யாவது? ... உயர்நிலை உலகத்து நுகர்ப), while 777 names only fame (சுழலும் இசை). The contrast is real, but the teaches sentence turns on what a commentator added, which is outside both verses, so the pairing's lesson rests on commentary rather than the Tamil.

Both redefine who has eyes: கண்ணுடையர் என்பவர் கற்றோர் (393) and கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர் (577). The same title is granted on two tests, learning and kindly regard, a real pattern across two domains, and the teaches sentence states it without inventing a conflict.

Both Paranar poems cite the cloak given to the peacock (படா அம் மஞ்ஞைக்கு ஈத்த 141.11; படாஅம் ஈத்த 145.2). In 141 it proves giving without eye to the next world (மறுமை நோக்கின்றோ அன்றே), in 145 it is leverage for the woman in sorrow (இன்னாது உறைவி அரும்படர் களைமே). The poem does not call her his wife; that comes from tradition, but the teaches sentence holds without it.

Both show a drinker lying in the front yard (சீயா முன்றில் 316.2; முன்றில் கிடந்த பெருங்களி யாளற்கு 317.2) who has given away (316: pawned sword for guests; 317: gave to everyone, யார்க்கும் ஈய்ந்து). But 317 does not say he gave away his bedding: the speaker asks others to give him a hide or mat, and the poem is badly gapped, so the shared portrait rests on few surviving words.

Both friends refuse the man after his river-play with another woman and measure the gossip by Chezhiyan's Koodal: 116 by the shout on the battlefield (கூடற் பறந்தலை ... ஆர்ப்பினும் பெரிதே), 296 by the city's everyday clamour (கூடல் நீடிய மலிதரு கம்பலை போல). The pair shows one city serving as the scale in war and in peace, which neither poem shows alone.

Both address the house with புல்என் றனையால் (261.19; 250.6). In 261 the widow with shorn head is the simile (கொய்ம்மழித் தலையொடு ... மகடூஉப் போல), in 250 she is in the house (கூந்தல் கொய்து ... மனைவியொடு). The observation that one picture moves between vehicle and tenor is specific and true.

1055 grounds standing before others to ask (கண்ணின்று இரப்பவர்) in the existence of those who do not hide (கரப்பிலார்); 54 shows suppliants entering 'as if they owned it', heads high (உடையோர் போல ... அண்ணாந்து புகுதல்), because Kothai gives without stint (ஆனாது ஈயும்). The poem extends the couplet's premise into the asker's bearing and adds the rival kings' dread, as the teaches sentence says.

215's prediction that Pisiron will not stay away in trouble (அல்லற் காலை நில்லலன்) does match 238's vow to hurry to a friend in distress (முட்டுற்ற போழ்தின் முடுகி). But the teaches sentence rests on the tradition that the friend came to die with the king, which this poem never states; it is a prediction, not a case of the oath kept.

The only link is the word பசி: 13 says drought lets hunger torment the world, 225 ranks removing hunger above enduring it (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பசிஆற்றல்). 225 does not extend 13's thought about rain, and the ascetic reading the teaches relies on comes from commentators. This is a shared word dressed as development.

Both name the aims wealth yields: அறனும் பொருளும் இன்பமும் மூன்றும் ஆற்றும் நின்செல்வம் (28.15-16) and அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும் (754). 754 conditions it on how wealth was gained (திறனறிந்து தீதின்றி வந்த); 28 blames failure on போற்றாமை, neglect, which is not plainly 'spending'. The getting/spending contrast is suggestive but leans on a reading of a poem the marker flagged as uncertain.

174 names Mullur as the hill truthful-tongued Kapilan sang (பொய்யா நாவிற் கபிலன் பாடிய ... முள்ளூர் மீமிசை), and 123 is a Kapilar poem with முள்ளூர் மீமிசை, so the reference is real. But 174 does not develop 123's idea of sober giving; it cites the hill's sung fame. That it cites this very poem, and that Kapilar made Mullur's renown, goes beyond the Tamil.

Both are foster-mother laments after elopement in the same thurai. 153 dwells on the girl trusting a hard man (வன்க ணாளன் ... இன்சொற் பிணிப்ப நம்பி) and her feet (நல் அடிக்கு அமைந்த அல்ல); 145 curses her own hand that beat the girl (அஞ்ஞையை அலைத்த கையே). The outward/inward contrast is apt, but neither poem develops the other, so it is a pairing within one convention rather than a development.

Both are Paranar on Pekan. In 142 rain is the explicit figure for undiscriminating giving (வரையா மரபின் மாரி போல). In 262 the rain is literal spray on his hill (நுண்பல துவலை புதல்மிசை நனைக்கும் ... கொண்டல் மாமலை) whose smell is on her voice; giving appears only in the epithet வண்மகிழ். Calling this the praise-image reused stretches a landscape detail.

173's maxim says keeping dharma and propping up kin are not for those who sit idle (வருந்தா உள்ளமொடு இருந்தோர்க்கு இல்); it never names wealth, which the reader must infer from செய்வினை. 247's premise (பொருளில்லார்க்கு இவ்வுலகம் இல்லாகி) is only the vehicle of its comparison. The connection is real but needs that inference.

Both tie Thondi to its backwater neythal: மாக்கழி மலர்ந்த நெய்த லானும் ... தொண்டி (48.3-4) and தொண்டி முன்துறைச் ... பெருந்தண் நெய்தல் (290.13-14). The akam poet uses it as the beauty her eyes have lost (மணிஏர் மாண்நலம் ஒரீஇப் பொன்நேர் வண்ணம்). The note says what the akam poet does with the place, and the teaches sentence is specific.

In both moothin mullai poems the wife feeds bards and guests (பாணர் ஆர்த்தவும் பரிசிலர் ஓம்பவும் 334.6; வருவிருந்து அயரும் விருப்பினள் 326.12) and the husband has the gold plate from a war elephant's face (புகர்முகத்து அணிந்த பொலம் 334.8-9; யானை அணிந்த பொன்செய் ஓடை 326.14-15). Two poets building the house from the same pair of acts is a real finding; 'required' overstates slightly.

Pazhaiyan is named in both: fallen in 44 (பழையன் பட்டென, 11), and in 186 his Por on the Kaviri is the likeness for bangles never broken (பழையன் காவிரி வைப்பின் போஒர் அன்ன ... செறிவளை உடைத்தலோ இலனே). The name link is real, but neither poem places itself before or after his fall, so 'before and after' is not in the Tamil.

52 measures glory by the enemy's land turned to jungle (காடாகி விளியும் நாடு); 57 permits plunder, fire and killing but forbids felling the guarded trees (கடிமரம் தடிதல் ஓம்பு). The limit is real, but the reason 57 gives is practical (யானைக்குக் கந்தாற் றாவே), not sanctity, and the poems address different kings, so the claim about what poets held 'more inviolable than the lives of the conquered' overreaches.

24 closes with the saying that those who truly lived are those who did not go as the many go but died with lasting fame (வல்லுநர் வாழ்ந்தோர் என்ப ... பலர்செலச் செல்லாது நின்று விளிந் தோரே); 240 says those without renown do not live (இசையொழிய வாழ்வாரே வாழா தவர்). The என்ப marks it as an attributed saying placed after a blessing of pleasure, which is the specific point.

1151 refuses comfort in sharp words (செல்லாமை உண்டேல் எனக்குரை ... வாழ்வார்க் குரை), and in 5 she says nothing (முகத்தின் உரையா) and the sign is the garland on the son wilting under her breath (பிணையல் மோயினள் உயிர்த்த காலை ... அணியழி தோற்றம்), which stops him (கடிந்தனம், செலவே). The couplet's speaker is disputed, but the contrast of word and silence holds.

1261 has the woman's fingers worn by marking the days (நாளொற்றித் தேய்ந்த விரல்); 351 puts the same daily count of marks on the wall into the returning man's mind (செய்குறி ஆழி வைகல்தோறு எண்ணி எழுதுசுவர்). The pair shows the tally known from both sides, which neither verse shows alone.

Both Avvaiyar poems for Anji run a catalogue of the same arms, even to the bloodied hooves (மறுக்குளம் பினவே 97.13; மறுக் குளம்பின் 98.6): 97 counts the damage to his own weapons, 98 the enemy's defensive acts (மதிற் கதவம் எழுச் செல்லவும், புண்படு குருதி அம்பு ஒடுக்கவும்). 97's demand for tribute to save the town (நெல்லின் செம்மல் மூதூர்) and 98's pity for the doomed fields fit together as the note says.

Both women do send a non-human messenger: the north wind (வாடை ... செல்மதி) and the crab (அலவ ... சொல்லல் வேண்டுமால்). But this is the same domain, not a parallel one, and the lesson that the messenger fits the land is just the general rule of karupporul, not something the pair teaches.

The closing lines are identical (அருகாது ஈயும் வண்மை / உரைசால் நெடுந்தகை ஓம்பும் ஊரே, 320.17-18 and 329.8-9) after different scenes (the hunter's yard, the frontier village with the hero-stone), with the preceding line varied (பரிசிலர்க்கு / இரவலர்க்கு). A detachable closing formula is a fair inference, though scribal repetition is also possible.

149's man refuses even easily won wealth (அரிதுசெய் விழுப்பொருள் எளிதினிற் பெறினும் வாரேன்) for her tears, and 155's man holds that virtue and independence come from wealth (இரண்டும் பொருளின் ஆகும்). The verdicts are opposed, but they are the stock pair of thurais (staying back and going), spoken in different situations, which the brief does not count as tension; 155's maxim is also reported by the woman, not said in the man's own voice.

151 does not give Nannan a bad name: it calls him பொலந்தேர் நன்னன் and counts kinship with him as a credential (நன்னன் மருகன் அன்றியும், நீயும் முயங்கற்கு ஒத்தனை மன்னே); the shut door (பாடுநர்க்கு அடைத்த கதவின்) belongs to the young Vicchi lord's hill. So there is no incompatible reputation to set against 152's giving Nannan (இசைநல் ஈகைக் களிறுவீசு), and the note misdescribes 151.

1268 has two clauses, the king's victory (வென்றீக வேந்தன்) and the evening at home (மனைகலந்து மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து). 354 shows both met in order: the king has won and raised his flag (வென்றுகொடி எடுத்தனன் வேந்தனும்), cattle return and herdsmen play their flutes, and the hero is urged home to her pallor. The poem unfolds the couplet as the teaches sentence says.

382 does offer praise as a weapon (நின் பகைஞர் கேட்டொறும் நடுங்க ஏத்துவென் ... பிறர் வேத்தவை), and 400 pairs the king's enemies with the hunger of dependants (தன்பகை கடிதல் அன்றியும் ... பசிப்பகை கடிதலும் வல்லன்). But nothing makes 400 the content of the song promised in 382, and 'the gift buys propaganda for exactly the two powers' overreaches, since 382 mentions only the enemies. 400 has gaps at lines 12 and 18.

Both turn on the hero-stone crowned with a peacock feather (பீலி சூட்டி, 264.3; நடுகல் பீலி சூட்டி, 232.3). In 232 the man who would not take a whole country is offered a little toddy (கொள்வன் கொல்லோ ... கொள்ளா தோனே), and in 264 the bards may still be coming, not knowing (இன்றும் வருங்கொல், பாணரது கடும்பே). Together they show the gift relation reversed from both ends.

The formula நெடுநா ஒண்மணி (24.13; Mullaippattu 50) and the roaring drum at the sleepless midnight camp (தழங்குகுரல் முரசமொடு முழங்கும் யாமத்து; முரசுமுழங்கு பாசறை, 79) are shared. The idyll's span gives the camp to the king, who lies awake thinking of the enemy (பகைவர்ச் சுட்டிய), while 24's speaker is a man in the camp (வேந்தன் பாசறை யேமே) whose wife waits. In the idyll the bell is stilled (நிழத்திய) at midnight, a difference the note omits.

114 does make evening the wife's grief (சிறுபுன் மாலையும் உள்ளார் ... நம்புலந்து உறையும் எவ்வம்) and has him urge the charioteer on. But the king's victory, 1268's first clause, is only in the colophon, and the watchmen's lamps already shine like stars (யாமம் கொள்பவர் நாட்டிய நளிசுடர்), so 'a race against dusk' does not fit the poem.

259's friend bids the girl bear her mother's grief (அன்னை அல்லல் தாங்கி), though who bears it is unclear; 55's mother quarrels with her life for not leaving to follow the girl (போதல் செல்லாஎன் உயிரொடு புலந்தே). The pair shows the elopement from two sides of one situation, but neither limits the other, so qualifies does not fit, and the link is mainly a shared situation.

The phrase உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் is shared exactly. In 1079 the base man faults others for their food and clothing; in 166 one who envies giving (கொடுப்பது அழுக்கறுப்பான்) loses food and clothing for his kin. The object of envy differs (others' goods versus another's gift), so 'what is envied returning as what is lost' joins the two only loosely.

769 lists poverty (வறுமை) among the things an army must be free of; 299 sets the small-village chief's gram-fed horse (உழுத்துஅதர் உண்ட) cleaving the front against the ghee-fed horses of rich kings that hang back. The poem's 'poverty' is a modest village chief, not an unpaid army, so the qualification needs a generous reading, though the teaches sentence is fair to both.

134 explicitly scorns giving on the reckoning that what is done here serves the next life (இம்மைச் செய்தது மறுமைக்கு ஆம் எனும் அறவிலை வணிகன் ஆஅய் அல்லன்), while Naladiyar 95 tells one to give looking to the next world and this (மறுமையும் இம்மையும் நோக்கி). That is a direct conflict over motive. 134 puts custom in its place (சான்றோர் சென்ற நெறி); 'honour' is the note's addition.

ullurai.anchor: வாளை மேய்ந்த வள்ளெயிற்று நீர்நாய் முள்ளரைப் பிரம்பின் மூதரில் செறியும்

poems.note: The otter sits inside the place-epithet of an open அன்ன comparison (கழாஅர் அன்ன எம் இளமை) whose stated tenor is her youth, not the husband, so condition 2 was read as passed; pairs: feeding on vaalai = his pleasure with the other woman, slinking into the old thicket = his return to the aged wife (எம் முதுமை எள்ளல்).
The ants' hoard is one item in a scene of a raided, ruined village; no one-sentence sense for the lovers can be fixed.

iraicchi.act: the male tiger listens for the stag's call to hunt for his tigress starving after giving birth
iraicchi.sense: even the tiger stays to feed his famished mate, while her man has gone and she wastes without food (உண்ணா உயக்கமொடு)

poems.note: The ox straining at the mired cart is the open vehicle of the stated sense (பகட்டின் வருந்தி வெய்ய உயிர்க்கும் நோய்), so striking it removes the sense.

iraicchi.act: the bull, wanting to stay together, embraces the young cow and goes home with her to the village at evening
iraicchi.sense: the hero, too, must reach his wife by evening, while she hears the herd come home and is left helpless

poems.note: The peacock is an open simile for her (போல).
The tortoise feeding on what flows from the upper ford and quivering like a drum yields no second correspondence to the friend's plea.
The poem states the comparison itself (குறியா இன்பம் ... குறித்த இன்பம் நினக்கெவன் அரிய?), so the monkey scene is open, not hidden.

iraicchi.act: the tall elephant that has lost its she-elephant trumpets on the slope, answering the thunder
iraicchi.sense: the man crossing that land will feel his own loss of her and long to return, so the friend tells the heroine not to despair

poems.note: The birds leaving the nest are an open simile (ஆங்கு) for her life leaving the body.

iraicchi.act: the otter rises to fetch the day's food for its unfed mate lying with the cub
iraicchi.sense: the lord, like the otter, is bound to feed his own wife and child at home, which is the courtesan's barb at the house-courtesan's hold on him

poems.note: The otter could also be read as a scene with parts, but only the one act (feeding the nursing mate) carries a clear sense.
The deserted village is description of the place he would sleep in; the doves leave because the house fell, not by an act that maps onto a person.
Puram anthology poem (colophon thinai பெருந்திணை), answered null per the rule for puram poems.
The elephant goring the tiger and seizing the millet field gives only one firm match (the hero braving danger); the owl is an open simile (ஆங்கு).
The wind is addressed directly, so striking it removes the poem.

iraicchi.act: the lone old stag, fooled by the mirage and worn out, will not leave its land but stays suffering in the hot forest
iraicchi.sense: even the beast does not leave its ground in hardship, yet he left her for a distant land

poems.note: The rain-softened ploughed soil is an open simile (போல்).

ullurai.anchor: மடிதுயில் முனைஇய ... நுங்கின் கள்ளின் ... மகிழ்புஇயங்கு நடையொடு ... ஆம்பல் மெல்அடை ஒடுங்கும்

iraicchi.act: the stag whose mate was shot thinks of her, refuses grazing and water and lies down grieving
iraicchi.sense: as the stag mourns its lost mate, so his beloved will weep more than he does, and he fears for her eyes
